historical_timeline.summary: Born Mary Jane Grant in Kingston, Jamaica.
Widowed; her mother dies soon after.
Nurses victims of cholera in Kingston.
Treats cholera in Cruces, Panama, and has cholera herself.
Supervises nursing during the yellow fever epidemic in Kingston.
Runs the British Hotel near Balaclava in the Crimean War.
Returns in poor health; declared bankrupt.
Seacole Fund festival; publishes her memoir.
Back in London; masseuse to the Princess of Wales.
Dies at home in Paddington after an apoplexy two weeks earlier.
Statue unveiled at St Thomas' Hospital.

claims.statement: She was born Mary Jane Grant in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1805, the daughter of James Grant, a white Scottish army officer, and a free Black Jamaican woman who kept a boarding house; she was born free, at a time when many Black people in the Caribbean were enslaved, and had a sister, Louisa, and a brother, Edward. In her memoir she wrote that "the century and myself were both young together" and called herself a Creole "with good Scotch blood."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the true birth year and the alias.

source_links.locator: SEACOLE, Mary (1805-1881); Born in Jamaica, Mary Jane Grant was the daughter of a Scottish soldier and a Creole hotel-keeper
Although Mary's mother was black, her father James Grant was a white Scottish army officer and Mary was born a 'free person'. She had a sister, Louisa, and a brother, Edward
I was born in the town of Kingston, in the island of Jamaica; the century and myself were both young together; I am a Creole, and have good Scotch blood coursing in my veins
roster birth year 1805

claims.statement: A London commemorative database gives her date of birth as November 23, 1805; English Heritage, the Mary Seacole Trust and her memoir give no day.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Used only to choose the month and day of the synthetic date of birth.

source_links.locator: As a female, and a widow, I may be well excused giving the precise date of this important event

claims.statement: Her mother was a healer, "like very many of the Creole women, an admirable doctress," and taught her traditional Jamaican medicine; as a child she practised on her doll, and she later learned "a great deal of Creole medicinal art" in her mother's house. She visited England in the early 1820s and gained some knowledge of European medicine.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her own healing knowledge, which the modern clinicians respect and ask about.

source_links.locator: My mother kept a boarding-house in Kingston, and was, like very many of the Creole women, an admirable doctress; learning a great deal of Creole medicinal art

she was also a healer and taught Mary many of her skills using traditional Jamaican medicines; It was an opportunity to acquire knowledge about modern European medicine which supplemented her training in traditional Caribbean techniques
She took a keen interest in her mother's work as a healer and later inherited her boarding house business

claims.statement: She married Edwin Horatio Hamilton Seacole on November 10, 1836, and they kept a store at Black River; he was delicate, she nursed him, and he died in 1844, followed closely by the death of her mother. She had no children.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her widowhood and living alone in the modern social history.

source_links.locator: Mary married Edwin Horatio Hamilton Seacole on 10th November 1836. They set up a store at Black River, but Edwin became unwell and delicate; Sadly, Edwin died in 1844, followed closely by the death of her mother; Mary had no children of her own
In 1836 she married Edwin Horatio Seacole ... but she was widowed eight years later
I kept him alive by kind nursing and attention as long as I could

claims.statement: In 1850 she nursed victims of the cholera epidemic in Kingston, learning about its treatment from a doctor lodging in her house; in 1851 she went to Cruces, on the Isthmus of Panama, where she treated cholera with mustard emetics, warm fomentations, mustard plasters and calomel, and was called the "yellow doctress."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her experience as a healer of epidemic disease.

source_links.locator: in 1850, she nursed victims of the Kingston cholera epidemic. travelling to Panama in 1851 only to find that her skills were needed once again because the town of Cruces was suffering its own outbreak; mustard emetics ... mustard plasters on the stomach and the back; Calomel

In the year 1850, the cholera swept over the island of Jamaica; received many hints as to its treatment; by dint of mustard emetics, warm fomentations, mustard plasters on the stomach and the back, and calomel; their 'yellow doctress' had the cholera
Seacole nursed patients during cholera epidemics in Jamaica and Panama

claims.statement: In Cruces she had cholera herself: "I felt an unpleasant chill come over me … and, before nightfall, I knew full well that my turn had come at last, and that the cholera had attacked me." She recovered.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own account of a serious past illness; recorded in the past medical history.

source_links.locator: CHAPTER IV ... THE CHOLERA ATTACKS ME; I felt an unpleasant chill come over me, and went to bed at once. Other symptoms followed quickly, and, before nightfall, I knew full well that my turn had come at last, and that the cholera had attacked me

claims.statement: In 1853 she cared for victims of a yellow fever epidemic in Kingston; she was invited by the medical authorities to supervise nursing at Up-Park Camp, the British Army's headquarters, and turned her mother's former lodging house into a hospital.

source_links.locator: In 1853, Mary returned to Kingston, caring for victims of a yellow fever epidemic. She was invited by the medical authorities to supervise nursing services at Up-Park
the yellow fever never made a more determined effort to exterminate the English in Jamaica than it did in that dreadful year
During a yellow fever epidemic in Jamaica, she helped organise medical care in a British military camp

claims.statement: At the outbreak of the Crimean War she went to London and asked the War Office to send her as an army nurse; she was refused. She paid her own way to the Crimea and, with Thomas Day, a relative of her husband, built the British Hotel at Spring Hill near Balaclava, a place of respite for sick and recovering soldiers; she nursed the wounded on the battlefield, sometimes under fire, and soldiers called her "Mother Seacole."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her public work and strengths. The refusal is recorded without speculation about its reasons.

source_links.locator: approached the British War Office, asking to be sent as an army nurse to the Crimea; She was refused. Undaunted, she funded her own trip to Crimea; established the British Hotel with Thomas Day, a relative of her husband; Mary's hotel near Balaclava; sometimes under fire; they called her 'Mother Seacole'
Spring Hill--so we christened our new home; the British Hotel
Mary Seacole left the Caribbean for England, where she arrived in late 1854

claims.statement: She returned from the Crimea in 1856 in poor health and poor finances; in her memoir she wrote: "I returned from it shaken in health … a little labour fatigues me now--I cannot watch by sick-beds as I could--a week's want of rest quite knocks me up now." She described herself as "a hearty, strong woman--plain-spoken people might say stout."
claims.clinical_interpretation: The only account of her health after the Crimea in the sources read; it names no diagnosis.

source_links.locator: To be sure, I returned from it shaken in health; for a little labour fatigues me now--I cannot watch by sick-beds as I could--a week's want of rest quite knocks me up now; I was always a hearty, strong woman--plain-spoken people might say stout
arriving in August 1856 with poor health and poor finances

claims.statement: With unpaid bills and unsold stock at the end of the war, she was declared bankrupt in November 1856. The Times and Punch campaigned for her, a Seacole Fund Grand Military Festival was held in Kennington in July 1857, and her autobiography, Wonderful Adventures of Mrs. Seacole in Many Lands, was published the same month.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her experience of financial hardship, which informs the modern discussion of costs.

source_links.locator: She was declared bankrupt in November that year, prompting campaigns by The Times and Punch in particular to reimburse her for her losses; In July 1857 a Seacole Fund Grand Military Festival was held in Kennington
In 1857 a fund-raising gala was held for her over four nights on the banks of the River Thames. Over 80,000 people attended
Then I returned bankrupt in fortune

claims.statement: W. H. Russell, war correspondent of The Times, wrote of her in 1857: "I trust that England will not forget one who nursed her sick, who sought out her wounded to aid and succour them, and who performed the last offices for some of her illustrious dead."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Public recognition of her work; strengths.

source_links.locator: I trust that England will not forget one who nursed her sick, who sought out her wounded to aid and succour them, and who performed the last offices for some of her illustrious dead

claims.statement: She travelled between England and Jamaica in the 1860s and was back in London by about 1869 to 1870, where she mixed with royalty and acted as a personal masseuse to the Princess of Wales; she was painted by Albert Charles Challen around 1869 and sculpted by Count Gleichen in 1871.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her life in London in the 1870s and her skill in massage. The two sources give 1869 and 1870 for her return.

source_links.locator: Seacole travelled to and fro between England and Jamaica during the 1860s but was back in London by 1869. She mixed increasingly with royalty, acting as a personal masseuse to the Princess of Wales, and in 1871 was sculpted by Count Gleichen
returning to London in 1870 where she mixed with some of her patrons; becoming a masseuse to Princess Alexandra
this portrait of Mary Seacole when she was around 65 years old

claims.statement: Her last known photograph was taken around 1873; little else is documented about her health or daily life in her last decade in London.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Records the gap in the documentary record for the years of the modern episode.

source_links.locator: This is the last picture of Mary, taken around 1873. The reason for its commission is unknown

claims.statement: Her memoir describes her lifelong practice of nursing and healing, including the remedies she carried, and her belief that the Creoles seek out "the simple remedies which are available for the terrible diseases": "beside the nettle ever grows the cure for its sting."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors respect for her own remedies in the modern episode.

source_links.locator: inducing them to seek out the simple remedies which are available for the terrible diseases by which foreigners are attacked; So true is it that beside the nettle ever grows the cure for its sting
samples of plants and herbs that Mary is likely to have carried in her medicine bag

claims.statement: She died on May 14, 1881, at her home in Paddington, London, aged about 75; a literary history records that she had suffered "an apoplexy" two weeks before and spent three days in a coma, that she died in prosperous circumstances with an estate of more than £2,500, and that she was buried, as she had asked, in the Roman Catholic section of Kensal Green Cemetery.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History after the modern episode. The cause rests on one scholarly secondary source; the death record itself was not read.

source_links.locator: 14 May 1881 MS died in prosperous circumstances. She had suffered an apoplexy two weeks before this, and spent three days in a coma. Her grave lies as she requested in the Roman Catholic section of Kensal Green Cemetery in London. Her estate amounted to more than £2,500
Ten years later she died at her home in Paddington
Died at home, 2 Cambridge Gardens, Paddington
roster death year 1881

claims.statement: "Apoplexy" in nineteenth-century usage meant a sudden loss of consciousness and is usually read today as a stroke; whether hers was a hemorrhage or an infarct, and what caused it, cannot be known from the sources.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective reading of the recorded term; it anchors the stroke-prevention teaching in the modern episode but is not a diagnosis.

source_links.locator: She had suffered an apoplexy two weeks before this, and spent three days in a coma

claims.statement: She was largely forgotten for about a century, until Caribbean nurses visited her grave; in 2004 she was voted the greatest Black Briton, and in 2016 a statue of her was unveiled at St Thomas' Hospital in London. The Mary Seacole Trust continues her legacy.

source_links.locator: she was then lost to history for around 100 years until nurses from the Caribbean visited her grave; In 2004, Mary was voted the Greatest Black Briton; In 2016, the statue was finally unveiled in the grounds of St Thomas' Hospital

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Hypertension with knee osteoarthritis and fall risk in a 71-year-old Black Jamaican British woman, a nurse and healer living alone in London on a modest fixed income. The episode covers a very high blood pressure found at a visit for headaches, without a hypertensive emergency; confirmation with home readings; baseline tests (metabolic panel, lipids, hemoglobin A1c, TSH, urine albumin, ECG, fundi and an echocardiogram for stage 2 hypertension); two first-line medicines of different classes, a calcium channel blocker and a thiazide-like diuretic, chosen under the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline, with a target below 130/80 mmHg; thiazide-associated hyponatremia and orthostatic hypotension with a near-fall during a cold, and the change to an angiotensin receptor blocker; a moderate-intensity statin; stroke risk reduction; knee osteoarthritis managed under the ACR/AF 2019 guideline with exercise therapy, tai chi, topical diclofenac, weight loss, a cane and an injection offered; falls under CDC STEADI and the USPSTF; bone health; her own healing knowledge and remedies respected and checked for interactions (liquorice root raises blood pressure and lowers potassium); loneliness and the cost of care; and her public work. It is taught with dignity and attention to equity: her expertise as a healer is respected, she is addressed as she wishes, and access barriers (cost of a cuff, transport, stairs) are solved rather than blamed on her.

visit_schedule.purpose: Visit for headaches on waking and knee pain with a fall: very high blood pressure found, without target-organ emergency; examination, ECG, laboratory tests, home monitoring, knee osteoarthritis, falls screen, her own remedies, and geriatric medicine referral

Same-day sick visit for dizziness on standing during a cold
Three-month review after chlorthalidone was stopped: blood pressure above target, losartan added; lipids on atorvastatin; knee and falls
Six-month review: blood pressure at target, screening and bone density results, knee function, falls and social connection

She has kept taking both blood pressure tablets, because she did not think a cold counted as being unable to eat; she has had no vomiting or diarrhea. She has no confusion, headache, chest pain, palpitations, weakness or numbness. She has not taken liquorice, which she paused at her first visit, or any cold remedies from the chemist. As a nurse she noticed her own pulse was fast and her mouth dry.

assessment.assessment: Stage 2 hypertension, confirmed at home, with ECG evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy and a 10-year cardiovascular risk of about 14%. She is fit, independent and has no orthostatic drop, so the target of below 130/80 mmHg applies to her as to younger adults, reached gradually. Start two first-line medicines: amlodipine 5 mg and chlorthalidone 12.5 mg. In a 71-year-old woman a thiazide can lower sodium, especially when she eats little, so check sodium and potassium in about four weeks, check standing pressure at every visit, and teach a sick-day rule to stop chlorthalidone if she cannot eat or drink normally. If sodium falls, stop it and use an angiotensin receptor blocker instead. An echocardiogram is reasonable for stage 2 hypertension with ECG voltage

STEADI shows high risk: a fall last year, fear of falling, a Timed Up and Go of 15 seconds, a below-average chair stand and poor tandem balance. No orthostatic drop, no sedating or anticholinergic medicines, and her vision is adequate. The stairs to her rooms and worn slip-on shoes are the main hazards. Strength and balance exercise reduces falls in community-dwelling older adults

Clinical bilateral knee osteoarthritis; imaging is not needed. Exercise therapy, then tai chi, topical diclofenac, weight loss of at least 5%, and a cane in the right hand are all strongly recommended. Avoid oral anti-inflammatory medicines, which raise blood pressure and harm the kidneys. An intra-articular corticosteroid injection is an option for a flare. Her own massage is welcome and fits the exercise plan

Liquorice root contains glycyrrhizin, which raises blood pressure and lowers potassium; that would add to the potassium loss from chlorthalidone, so pausing it is wise. Ginger tea in food amounts is fine. Her liniment contains camphor and methyl salicylate; used on one knee, or at a different time from the diclofenac gel, and never under a heat pad, it is safe. Her knowledge of her remedies is good, and she should be asked about any new one rather than told to stop

PHQ-9 of 6 reflects loneliness and fear of falling rather than depression. A social prescribing link worker, a tai chi group and a lunch club address loneliness and falls together. An occupational therapy home visit for a stair rail and bath board. Generic medicines in 90-day supplies, a free blood pressure monitor and help with transport keep costs down
